el-01.title: What Kind of Language Is English?
explain: **English** is one of the most widely used languages in the world today. In this department we look at English not only as a tool for speaking and writing, but also at the structure of the language itself (**English linguistics**) and at what is written in it (**English literature**). This lesson sketches the big picture of what kind of language English is.

Linguistics groups languages by lineage. English is described as belonging to the **Germanic branch** of the **Indo-European family**. This means it is related to German and Dutch. Korean does not belong to this family, so the two languages differ greatly, both in vocabulary and in how sentences are built.
The most noticeable difference is **word order**. English basically orders its clauses **subject (S) - verb (V) - object (O)**. Korean usually orders them **subject - object - verb**.

explain.alt: Comparison of English and Korean word order. In the upper English row, from the left: The cat (S, subject), chased (V, verb), a mouse (O, object). In the lower Korean row, from the left: 고양이가 (S, subject), 쥐를 (O, object), 쫓았다 (V, verb).

explain: Korean attaches particles such as "가" and "를" to show who the subject is and what the object is. So "고양이가 쥐를 쫓았다" and "쥐를 고양이가 쫓았다" differ in usage but state the same fact. English has almost no such particles, so **position** shows the role. In *The cat chased a mouse.* (the cat chased a mouse), swapping the two nouns gives *A mouse chased the cat.*, and the chaser and the chased trade places.

How did English spread so widely? No single cause explains it, but the following factors are commonly cited.
- Over many years Britain traded with and colonized many regions, spreading English.
- In the 20th century, American economic power, science, and popular culture broadened the use of English.
- In international trade, scholarship, and the internet, people with different native languages chose English as a common language.

For this reason it is often said that more people use English as a second or foreign language than as a native language. English also has different pronunciations and words in different regions, and no one of them is the "real" English.

English has also borrowed many words from other languages. *Restaurant* came from French, *piano* from Italian, and *kindergarten* from German. Taking in words this way is called **borrowing**. The Korean words "컴퓨터" (computer) and "버스" (bus) are likewise borrowed from English.

examples.title: An example of word order changing meaning
body: *The dog bit the man.* describes a situation in which the dog bit a person. *The man bit the dog.*, with the two nouns swapped, describes a person biting a dog. The words are exactly the same; only the word order changed. This shows how strongly word order decides meaning in English.

Translated into Korean, these are "개가 사람을 물었다" (the dog bit the person) and "사람이 개를 물었다" (the person bit the dog). In Korean the meaning differs because the positions where the particles "가" and "를" attach change. English and Korean make the same distinction by different means.

el-02.title: Sounds and Spelling
explain: What often surprises people who are learning English for the first time is that letters and sounds do not match one to one. In Hangul, one letter generally gives a fixed sound, but the English alphabet has only 26 letters while English has far more sounds. So the same letter can give several sounds, and the same sound can be written with several spellings.

First, some terms. **Spelling** is the way a word is written in letters, and **pronunciation** is the way the word is spoken. The Hangul sound notations in this lesson are only **approximations** close to English sounds, not exact pronunciations. Sounds cannot be played on this screen, so check the actual sound in a dictionary's pronunciation guide or by listening to a native speaker.

explain.alt: Two relationships between spelling and sound. In the upper part, arrows go from the letter c to two words: cat is labeled with the first sound ㅋ (approximate), and city with the first sound ㅅ (approximate). In the lower part, arrows from the three words see, sea, and key converge on a single box labeled [iː], a long "이" (approximate), meaning the three words share the same vowel sound.

explain: As in the figure, *c* is a sound close to Hangul ㅋ (like /k/) in *cat* and close to ㅅ (like /s/) in *city*. Conversely, *see*, *sea*, and *key* are spelled differently but have the same vowel sound.

Why did they drift apart? The commonly offered explanation is this. English pronunciation changed over many years, while spelling became somewhat fixed as printing spread. Pronunciation kept changing afterward, but the spelling stayed, so many words keep traces of older pronunciation. For example, the *k* and the *gh* in *knight* are now **silent letters**. When words were borrowed from other languages, the original spelling was also often left as it was.

Still, there are not no rules at all. A typical example is the *e* at the end of a word. In many words, when a silent *e* is added at the end, the preceding vowel changes to a long sound close to the "name of the letter."
- *cap* (close to Korean "캡") → *cape* (close to "케이프")
- *kit* (close to "킷") → *kite* (close to "카이트")
There are also many exceptions. So when you meet a new word, it is a good habit to guess the sound from the spelling but check the pronunciation guide if you are not sure.

examples.title: Finding the silent letters
body: In *knee* (the joint of the leg), the *k* is not read, and the word sounds close to *nee*. In *lamb* (a young sheep), the *b* is not read. In *write*, the *w* is not read, and in *island*, the *s* is not read.
Even if these letters seem useless, it is often explained that spelling carries the history the word has traveled.

el-03.title: Sentence Structure: Parts of Speech and the Five Sentence Patterns
explain:
To understand a sentence, you must distinguish the kinds of words and the roles they play in the sentence. The kinds into which words are divided by grammatical properties are called **parts of speech**. The parts of speech commonly used at the introductory level are as follows.
- **Noun**: the name of a person, thing, or concept (*teacher*, *idea*)
- **Pronoun**: a word that stands in for a noun (*she*, *it*)
- **Verb**: an action or state (*run*, *is*)
- **Adjective**: modifies or describes a noun (*happy*, *red*)
- **Adverb**: modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb (*quickly*, *very*)
- **Preposition**: placed before a noun to show position, direction, and so on (*in*, *on*)
- **Conjunction**: joins words or sentences (*and*, *but*)

The same word can belong to a different part of speech depending on how it is used. The *run* in *a run* (a jog) is a noun, and the *run* in *I run* is a verb. A part of speech is less a label attached to the word itself than a use within the sentence.

Next come the **roles** within a sentence, that is, sentence elements. The **subject** is the main actor of the sentence, the **verb** is its action or state, the **object** is the target that receives the action, and the **complement** is a word that supplements what the subject or object is.

Traditional English grammar divides the basic frame of a sentence into five types according to the elements required. These are called the **five sentence patterns**. This method is widely used in school grammar, and note that some modern grammar books divide the frames differently.

explain.alt: Five sentence frames. Pattern 1: Birds (S) sing (V). Pattern 2: She (S) is (V) happy (C). Pattern 3: I (S) read (V) a book (O). Pattern 4: He (S) gave (V) me (IO) a gift (DO). Pattern 5: We (S) call (V) him (O) Sam (OC). Below is a legend: S subject, V verb, O object, C complement, IO indirect object, DO direct object, OC object complement.

explain: Pattern 1 forms a sentence with just a subject and a verb. In Pattern 2, the complement after the verb describes the subject (*She = happy*). In Pattern 3, one object follows the verb. In Pattern 4, an indirect object corresponding to "to whom" and a direct object corresponding to "what" follow in turn. In Pattern 5, an object complement follows the object and describes it (*him = Sam*).

examples.title: Taking a sentence apart
body: In *She gave me a gift.*, She is the subject, gave is the verb, me is the indirect object (the person who receives the gift), and a gift is the direct object (the thing given). This is Pattern 4.

In *They elected her captain.*, They is the subject, elected is the verb, her is the object, and captain is the object complement. Since there is a relationship "she = the captain" between her and captain, this is Pattern 5.

el-04.title: Tense and Aspect: The Present Perfect
explain: **Tense** is a grammatical category that expresses time through the form of the verb. English verbs have distinct present (*walk*) and past (*walked*) forms. The future is expressed by placing expressions such as *will* or *be going to* in front. **Aspect** is a category that expresses in what manner an event unfolds and ends. The representative aspects are the **progressive** (*be + -ing*) and the **perfect** (*have + past participle*).

The **present perfect** (*have/has + past participle*) feels difficult because Korean has no grammatical form that corresponds to it exactly. The key point is that it **connects a past event to the present**. The simple past speaks of a past event cut off from now, while the present perfect carries the sense that the event continues up to now or affects the present.

explain.alt: Two timelines. In the upper one, for the sentence I lived there in 2015., a marker for a finished event sits in a short stretch between the past and the present and ends before the present line. In the lower one, for the sentence I have lived here for five years., a period running from a point in the past to the present line is shaded and labeled as a period that continues up to now.

explain:
The present perfect is commonly divided into three meanings.
- **Continuation**: begins in the past and continues now. *I have lived here for five years.*
- **Experience**: has happened at least once up to now. *I have been to Jeju twice.*
- **Result**: the result of a past event remains now. *She has lost her phone.* (She lost her phone, and she does not have it now.)

There is a point to watch. The present perfect is not used with words that pinpoint a finished time, such as *yesterday*, *last year*, or *in 2015*. For such times, the simple past is used. *I saw him yesterday.* is correct, but *I have seen him yesterday.* is wrong. Conversely, *for* (during), *since* (from then until now), *ever* (at any time up to now), and *just* (a moment ago) go well with the present perfect.

examples.title: Comparing the simple past and the present perfect
body: *I lost my key.* only states the past event of losing a key and does not tell whether it has been found now. *I have lost my key.* also conveys the present situation that the key is missing now.
*I lived there in 2015.* is a simple past that names the finished time, 2015. *I have lived here for five years.* is a present perfect that began five years ago and continues to the present.

el-05.title: Reading Literature: Speaker and Figurative Language
explain: Literary works do not stop at conveying information; through the way they speak, they let us feel an experience. The first question to ask when reading a poem is "Who is speaking?" The voice that speaks within a poem is called the **speaker**. The speaker may be the same person as the author, but may also be a character created within the work. So rather than jumping to the conclusion that "the person who wrote the poem thought this," we first read it as something the speaker says.
Below is a short poem written for this lesson. Its title is *Last Bus*.

explain.alt: A short English poem titled Last Bus. Line 1: I ride the last bus home. Line 2: The window holds my face. Line 3: like a lantern on black water. Line 4: The city is a sleeping animal, Line 5: and I, a thought it forgot to finish.

explain: Put in plain words, it goes roughly like this: "I ride the last bus home. The window holds my face, like a lantern on black water. The city is a sleeping animal, and I am a thought it forgot to finish."
The speaker is the "I" sitting on the bus, looking at his or her own face reflected in the window and at the city. Through this speaker's eyes the poem shows the city at night.

Poems create unfamiliar feelings through **figurative language**. Figurative language is a way of speaking of one thing by comparing it to another. There are two representative kinds.
- **Simile**: openly compares two things using a word such as *like* or *as*. Line 3, "my face ... like a lantern," is one.
- **Metaphor**: says "A is B" without a word of comparison. Line 4, "The city is a sleeping animal," is one.

explain.alt: Comparison of simile and metaphor. The simile row has three boxes, my face, like, a lantern, and notes that there is a word of comparison (like, as). The metaphor row has three boxes, the city, is, a sleeping animal, and notes that it states the identity directly with no word of comparison.

explain: When reading figurative language, ask two things: what is compared to what, and in what respect the two are alike. Comparing a face reflected in a dark window to a lantern brings to mind a bright face floating alone in the darkness. Comparing the city to a sleeping animal gives a feeling of a quiet, large mass. Such interpretations are not fixed to a single one; it is enough if the reader can state reasons for them.

examples.title: Reading one more example of figurative language
body: *Her laugh was as bright as a morning window.* is a simile using *as ... as*. Because the laugh is compared to a morning window, a feeling of brightness and clarity comes across.
*The classroom was a beehive.* is a metaphor joined with "was" and no word of comparison. It speaks of the classroom as a busy, buzzing place by comparing it to a beehive.

el-06.title: Reading Strategies and Short Writing
explain: If you look up every unknown word in a dictionary as you read English, the flow of your reading is broken. There is a method of guessing the meaning of an unknown word from the surrounding text. This is called using **context clues**. **Context** is the flow formed by the text before and after a word.

explain.alt: Guessing a word's meaning from context. The top sentence is The trail was so ______ that we kept resting. with a blank. Arrows run downward through boxes in this order: Clue: kept resting; Guess: the trail must have been hard and tiring; Check: put it in and read again.

explain:
The blank in the figure is filled by *arduous* (hard and tiring). Even without knowing this word, the clue "kept resting" lets you guess that the trail was hard. Context clues can be divided as follows.
- **Explanation**: the meaning is given after the word. *…, that is, …*
- **Contrast**: guess from words of opposite meaning. *but*, *however*
- **Example**: guess from the examples given. *such as*, *for example*
- **Cause and effect**: guess from the reason or the result. *so ... that*, *therefore*

The **structure** of a word is also a clue. A word can often be divided into pieces that carry meaning. *un-* adds "not" (*unhappy*), *re-* adds "again" (*rewrite*), *-less* adds "without" (*careless* = without care), and *-ful* adds "full of" (*careful*).

The steps for guessing meaning from context are as follows.
1. Read the sentence containing the unknown word to the end.
2. Look around the word for words that serve as clues.
3. Guess the meaning based on the clues.
4. Put the guessed meaning in and read again to check that it makes sense.

A guess is only an approximation, so it is best to check important words in a dictionary later. Now you will try writing, using what you have learned in this strand. The last question is an ungraded writing task.

examples.title: Guessing meaning from clues
body: In *Unlike her talkative brother, Mina is quite taciturn.*, *Unlike* signals a contrast. Her brother talks a lot, and Mina is said to be different from him, so you can guess that *taciturn* means something close to "saying little."
When there is *such as*, as in *He has a hobby such as stamp collecting.*, the words after it are an example of the words before it.

el-07.title: Non-finite Clauses: To-Infinitives, Gerunds, and Participles
explain: In the sentence *Mina decided to leave.*, *leave* has neither tense nor subject. Yet we understand at once that the one leaving is Mina. Explaining how a chunk led by a verb with no tense marking is interpreted within a sentence is the problem of this lesson. Understanding such chunks lets you read even long sentences like *Walking home, Jun saw a fox.* accurately.

First, the distinction. A **finite clause** is a clause with a verb that shows tense or agreement with its subject. The *decided* in *Mina decided* is in the past tense, and the *lives* in *Jun lives here* is in the present tense with the third-person singular -s. By contrast, the verb of a **non-finite clause** has a form that cannot express tense directly. There are four representative kinds.
- **To-infinitive**: *to leave*, *to read*
- **Bare infinitive**: the base form of a verb without to, like *carry* in *help her carry*
- **-ing form**: the gerund *swimming*, the present participle *walking*
- **-ed/-en form**: the past participle *finished*, *broken*

Because a non-finite clause has no tense, its time is read **relative to the main clause**. In *Mina decided to leave*, the leaving comes after the time of deciding, and in *Mina remembers meeting him*, the meeting comes before the time of remembering. Even with the same -ing form, the time relation to the main clause differs depending on the verb.

Next is the problem of finding the missing subject. A non-finite clause has no audible subject, but it has an understood subject. There are two basic principles. First, if there is an object, the object is often the understood subject. In *Jun wants **Mina** to leave*, the one who leaves is Mina. Second, if there is no object, the subject of the main clause is the understood subject. In *Jun wants to leave*, the one who leaves is Jun. Generative grammar sometimes represents this invisible subject with the symbol PRO, but for reading practice it is enough to ask, "Who performs this action?"

A **participial clause** is a case where this principle is especially noticeable. In *Walking home, Jun saw a fox.*, the understood subject of *Walking home* is Jun, the subject of the main clause. So if it does not match the subject of the main clause, it becomes awkward. *Walking home, a fox appeared.* reads as if the fox were walking home. Such a sentence is called a **dangling participle**. To fix it, either match the subjects (*Walking home, Jun saw a fox*) or rewrite the participial clause as a finite clause (*As Jun walked home, a fox appeared*).

Which non-finite form a verb requires is also fixed word by word. *Want*, *decide*, and *hope* take the to-infinitive (*decide to go*), and *enjoy*, *avoid*, and *finish* take the -ing form (*enjoy swimming*). Some verbs take both, but the meaning changes. *Mina remembered to lock the door.* means she did not forget and locked it, while *Mina remembered locking the door.* means she recalled the locking she had already done. The former refers to something still to be done, the latter to something already done.

Know the limits as well. The classification above (finite and non-finite, understood subject) is an area where traditional grammar and generative grammar use different names and explanations. Also, idiomatic participial clauses used regardless of the main clause subject, such as *Generally speaking, ...*, are usually not treated as dangling participles. Rather than memorizing rules, the important habit is to ask, when you meet a non-finite phrase, "Time is relative to the main clause; who is the subject?"

examples.title: Sorting finite and non-finite forms in one sentence
body: Given: *After finishing her homework, Mina decided to take a walk.*
Step 1: Find the finite verb first. *Decided* shows past tense, so it is the verb of the finite clause, and the main clause of this sentence is *Mina decided ...*.

Step 2: Find the verb forms with no tense. *Finishing* (the -ing form, after the preposition after) and *to take* (a to-infinitive) are non-finite. Both have the main clause subject Mina as their understood subject.

Interpretation: Finishing the homework comes before the deciding, and the walk comes after the deciding. The time order comes not from the form of the non-finite phrases but from the main clause vocabulary *after* and *decide to*.

examples.title: Fixing a dangling participle
body: Given: *Running for the bus, his bag fell off his shoulder.*
Step 1: Find the understood subject of *Running*. The subject of the main clause is *his bag*. Then the bag would be the one running for the bus.
Step 2: Fix it in two ways. (1) Match the subjects. *Running for the bus, he dropped his bag.* (2) Rewrite it as a finite clause. *As he ran for the bus, his bag fell off his shoulder.*
Interpretation: The intended meaning is that a person ran, so the sentence must be rebuilt so that the subject of the non-finite clause and the main clause subject are the same.

el-08.title: Wh-Movement and Auxiliary Inversion
explain: In *Mina will buy a book.*, *a book* comes right after the verb *buy*. But in *What will Mina buy?*, the question word *what* has gone to the very front of the sentence, and the place after *buy* is empty. Even so, the requirement that *buy* needs something to buy remains in force. This lesson deals with how to explain that "empty place."

Syntax explains this as **movement**. The question word is seen as originally generated in the object position, then moved to the front of the sentence, leaving a gap in its original position. There is evidence. *What will Mina buy a book?* is strange, because the object position of *buy* is already filled by *a book*. That is, *what* appears at the front but still plays the role of the object of *buy*.

explain.alt: Word-order comparison in two rows. The upper row, "declarative (basic order)," has four boxes: Mina, will, buy, what. The lower row, "question (surface order)," has four boxes: What, will, Mina, buy, and a dotted box at the far right labeled "( gap )." An orange curved arrow runs from the dotted box to the What box and is labeled "movement." Under the boxes in the lower row are the names wh-phrase, auxiliary, subject, and verb.

explain: Let us lay out the derivation in the figure in steps. (1) Build the basic order: *Mina will buy what*. (2) Move the wh-phrase to the front of the sentence: *What Mina will buy ___*. (3) Move the auxiliary in front of the subject (**auxiliary inversion**): *What will Mina buy ___?* When there is an auxiliary, it is flipped like this. The names under the boxes in the lower row of the figure label the elements changed in this process.

When there is no auxiliary, **do-insertion** occurs. In *Mina bought a book*, the element expressing tense is attached to the verb. Inversion requires an auxiliary, so *did* is inserted, and since *did* carries the tense, the main verb returns to its base form: *What did Mina buy?* (not *bought*). A yes/no question does only inversion, without wh-movement: *Will Mina buy a book?*, *Did Mina buy a book?* And a question about the subject needs neither inversion nor do-insertion: *Who bought a book?*

Relative clauses are explained by the same principle. In *the book that Mina bought ___*, the relative pronoun *that* (or *which*) is seen as having moved forward from the object position of *bought*. So filling the gap again, as in *the book that Mina bought it*, is awkward. This is because the object position is filled twice.

Movement has constraints. *What do you think Mina bought ___?* is natural, but *What did you hear the rumor that Mina bought ___?* is hard to accept. The **island constraint**, proposed in the late 1960s, says that it is hard to take an element out of structures such as a complex noun phrase (*the rumor that ...*). Also, not every language moves. In the Korean *민아는 무엇을 샀니?* (what did Mina buy?), the question word stays in place. English wh-movement is one way a language can work, and it differs from language to language.

examples.title: Forming a question about the object
body: Given: Form a question about Mina in *Jun saw Mina at the library.*
Step 1: Replace Mina with the wh-phrase *who* and move it to the front. *Who Jun saw ___ at the library.*
Step 2: Since there is no auxiliary, insert *did*, move it in front of the subject, and return the main verb to its base form. *Who did Jun see at the library?*
Interpretation: *Saw* became *see* because the tense moved to *did*. The gap is right after *see*, in the object position.

examples.title: Comparing a subject question and an object question
body: Given: In *Mina called Jun.*, ask about the subject and the object respectively.
Step 1 (subject): The position being asked about is already at the front of the sentence, so neither movement nor inversion is needed. *Who called Jun?*
Step 2 (object): The object moves to the front and do-insertion is needed. *Who did Mina call?*
Interpretation: Both questions begin with *who*, but their sentence structures differ. *Who did call Jun?* is not used unless it is an emphatic use.

el-09.title: Information Structure: Given and New Information and the Passive
explain: *Jo shared the cake.* and *The cake was shared by Jo.* describe the same event. Yet there are conversations in which one of them becomes awkward. This is because a sentence being grammatically correct is different from its being natural in that place. The area that deals with how sentences are arranged within discourse is **information structure**.

There are two basic concepts. **Given information** is content that has already been mentioned or can be known from the situation, and **new information** is content being told for the first time. English generally places given information first and new information later. The tendency to place new information at the end of a sentence is called the **end-focus principle**. This is because the end of a sentence is the most noticeable position.

explain.alt: A figure showing the components of three sentences as boxes. Sentence 1 consists of "A girl" (new, orange) and "arrived." Sentence 2 consists of "The girl" (given, green), "brought," and "a cake" (new, orange). Sentence 3 consists of "The cake" (given, green), "was shared," and "by Jo" (new, orange). Below is a legend: the label for given means given information, the label for new means new information, and a hyphen means a verb.

explain: Let us read the figure in sentence order. In sentence 1, *A girl* appears for the first time, so it is new information. In sentence 2, *The girl* has already been introduced, so it stands first as given information, and the newly told *a cake* comes at the end. In sentence 3, *the cake*, just introduced, stands in the subject position, and the new information *by Jo* comes at the end. This is a representative reason the passive is used. With the active sentence *Jo shared the cake*, the new information Jo would come first and the given information last.

Besides the passive, there are other tools that change the sentence pattern to arrange information. The **there-construction** introduces a new entity. *There is a cat on the roof.* A **cleft sentence** puts the focus on one element. *It was Jo who shared the cake.* expresses a contrast, "Jo and no one else." A **pseudo-cleft sentence** sends the focus to the end, as in *What Jo shared was the cake.* All of them are ways of telling the same event in a different information packaging.

In speech, focus is shown by **sentence stress**. *Jo shared the CAKE.* is natural as an answer to "What did they share?" and *JO shared the cake.* as an answer to "Who shared it?" This site does not play sound, so stress is marked with capital letters.

There are limits and exceptions too. Information placement is not the only reason the passive is used. It is also used when the agent is unknown or unimportant (*The window was broken.*). Also, one cannot simply assert that "a definite entity = given information." Something like *the sun* is treated like given information even when first mentioned, if it can be known from the situation. The school-grammar explanation that "the active and the passive mean the same" is right in terms of truth conditions but not in terms of information structure.

examples.title: Choosing the sentence pattern that fits the context
body: Given: In a conversation, "We were talking about Mina." Next, you want to describe the event *A dog ... Mina.*
Step 1: The given information is Mina, and the new information is a dog.
Step 2: To put the given information first and the new information at the end, the passive is natural. *Mina was chased by a dog.*
Interpretation: The active *A dog chased Mina.* is also grammatical, but in this context the new entity comes first and breaks the flow of the story.

examples.title: Contrastive focus in a cleft sentence
body: Given: A asks, *Tom shared the cake, right?*, and B wants to correct this.
Step 1: The information B wants to tell is Jo, which contrasts with the wrong information, Tom.
Step 2: B makes a contrastive focus with the cleft sentence *No, it was Jo who shared it.*
Interpretation: Simply saying *Jo shared it.* would also be understood, but the cleft sentence makes "not Tom" clear.

el-10.title: Old and Middle English and the Loss of Inflection
explain: Even people who use English today cannot read English writing from a thousand years ago. Yet the older forms of *house*, *moon*, and *father* still seem familiar. How did English come to look as it does now? The history of English is usually divided into **Old English** (about 450-1100), **Middle English** (about 1100-1500), **Early Modern English** (about 1500-1700), and **Modern English**. The boundary years are a convenience.

explain.alt: Four bars are joined along a horizontal time axis: Old English (about 450 to about 1100), Middle English (about 1100 to about 1500), Early Modern (about 1500 to about 1700), and Modern English (after about 1700). Above the bars, dotted lines mark three events: 1066 Norman Conquest, 1476 start of printing, 1755 Johnson's Dictionary.

explain: Old English developed from the speech of Germanic groups such as the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, who crossed to the island of Britain around the 5th century. This language was rich in **inflection**, in which nouns, adjectives, and articles change their endings according to **case** (nominative, accusative, genitive, dative) and gender. For example, basic words such as *cyning* (king), *hūs* (house), *mōna* (moon), *wæter* (water), and *fæder* (father) lead to today's *king*, *house*, *moon*, *water*, and *father*. When case shows in endings, one can tell who did what even if the word order is relatively free.

On the way to Middle English, the endings weakened and merged. Because stress tended strongly to fall at the beginning of a word, the vowels of final syllables came to be pronounced indistinctly and blended into one. Since endings could no longer signal case, other devices became necessary. Those devices were **fixed word order** (subject-verb-object) and **prepositions**. This is why the five sentence patterns learned in Stage 1 became the frame of English. The explanation connects like this: weakening of endings, loss of case markers, fixing of word order.

The Norman Conquest of 1066 greatly changed the vocabulary. For some time afterward, the ruling class of England used French (Norman French), and many words of politics, law, cooking, and art entered English. *Government*, *court*, *judge*, and *mansion* are examples. As a result, layers arose within the same area of meaning. Words for livestock are often of English origin (*cow*, *sheep*, *pig*) while words for the meat are of French origin (*beef*, *mutton*, *pork*). This is commonly explained by the social difference between those who raised the animals and the upper class at the table. In addition, contact with the Norse Vikings brought words such as *they*, *sky*, and *egg* into English.

Reading the layers of words reveals differences in style. For the same meaning there are several words, such as *ask* (an everyday word from Old English), *question* (of French origin), and *interrogate* (an academic word that keeps the Latin form directly). In general, the more everyday the word, the more Germanic it is, and the higher the formality, the more words of French or Latin origin increase. When Caxton began printing in England in the late 15th century, spelling gradually became fixed, and in the 18th century dictionaries served as a standard. This connects to the mismatch of spelling and pronunciation in a later lesson.

Limits: 1066 was not a turning point overnight. The weakening of inflectional endings was already under way before the Conquest and appeared first in the northern dialects. The explanation that "French pressed down on English and removed the endings" is also inaccurate. Moreover, Modern English still keeps traces of inflection: the case of pronouns (*he, him, his*), the plural -s, and the possessive -'s. The history of English should be read not as a linear story but as gradual change with several causes overlapping.

examples.title: Seeing why word order becomes fixed through a model
body: Given (hypothetical): In a certain language, the subject takes -a at the end of the word and the object takes -u. So *dog-a bites man-u* and *man-u bites dog-a* mean the same even though the word order differs.
Step 1: If the endings disappear, only *dog bites man* and *man bites dog* remain. Changing the word order reverses who bites.
Step 2: To avoid confusion of meaning, the word order must be fixed. English came to let subject-verb-object order and prepositions take over the role of case.
Interpretation: The actual history is far more complicated, but this model shows the logic that when case markers decrease, word order comes to carry the meaning.

examples.title: Telling the layers of words apart
body: Given: *The sheep became mutton on the table.*
Step 1: *Sheep* is an old word of English origin and refers to the living animal.
Step 2: *Mutton* is of French origin and refers to the meat of the same animal.
Interpretation: One sentence contains both Germanic and French layers. In this way, the lineage of each word carries the history of English.

el-11.title: The Great Vowel Shift and the Mismatch of Spelling and Pronunciation
explain: Why is the i in *bite* read like "eye" rather than "ee"? In Italian or German, i is generally read as "ee." There is a historical reason why English vowel spellings are read differently from other languages. At its center is the **Great Vowel Shift**. It was an event in which English **long vowels** changed systematically from late Middle English into Early Modern English. It is thought to have proceeded around the 15th century and continued into the 1600s (dates differ by scholar and dialect).

First, let us sort out long and short vowels. In a language where vowel length distinguishes meaning, a long vowel is one that is held longer. The : in symbols such as /iː/ below marks that the vowel is lengthened. This notation is the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), and a Hangul approximation is added beside it. The approximations are not identical to the actual sounds.

explain.alt: A table of five rows. The columns are word, earlier sound, later sound, and type of change. Bite goes from /iː/ (Hangul 비-) to /aɪ/ (Hangul 아이), diphthongization. Mouse goes from /uː/ (Hangul 무-) to /aʊ/ (Hangul 아우), diphthongization. Feet goes from /eː/ (Hangul 에-) to /iː/ (Hangul 이-), tongue raised. Moon goes from /oː/ (Hangul 오-) to /uː/ (Hangul 우-), tongue raised. Name goes from /aː/ (Hangul 아-) to /eɪ/ (Hangul 에이), tongue raised. Below is a note that the earlier sound is late Middle English and the later sound is Modern English (approximate).

explain: The five rows in the figure are the core of the change. The rule is simple. Long vowels with the tongue at a middle or low position **rose one step** (/eː/ → /iː/, /oː/ → /uː/, and /aː/ → /eɪ/, rising and becoming a diphthong). The highest long vowels, /iː/ and /uː/, had nowhere higher to go and split into **diphthongs** (/iː/ → /aɪ/, /uː/ → /aʊ/). As a result, Middle English *bite* /biːt/ became today's /baɪt/, and *mouse* /muːs/ became /maʊs/.

Why it happened is still not agreed upon. A **drag chain** explanation, in which the high vowels became diphthongs and left gaps that pulled the lower vowels up, competes with a **push chain** explanation, in which the lower vowels rose and pushed the high vowels out. Some explanations also cite social factors such as social mobility and dialect contact. No single position has settled as the answer.

The mismatch with spelling comes from the time lag between this change and printing. When printing began at the end of the 15th century, spelling still reflected the pronunciation from before the change. Sounds kept changing afterward, but spelling had become fixed. So the ee in *feet* was once /eː/, and the a in *name* was once /aː/. This explains why vowel letters in Old English had values similar to those in other European languages.

The Great Vowel Shift also leaves traces in the relations between words. *Sane* (/seɪn/) and *sanity*, *divine* (/dɪˈvaɪn/) and *divinity*, and *serene* and *serenity* are related words whose vowels differ. This is explained as the long vowel that underwent the shift becoming shortened in the derived word, so that the old short vowel remains.

There are exceptions and limits too. *Great*, *break*, and *steak* did not rise to /iː/ and remained /eɪ/. The extent of the change also differs by dialect, and in northern British dialects and others, part of it proceeded differently. Also, this event is not representative of all sound changes; it is one example, a systematic shift of long vowels. Other causes also contribute to the mismatch of English spelling, such as borrowed spellings from foreign languages and silent letters.

examples.title: Estimating today's sound from an older sound
body: Given: Late Middle English *town* was pronounced roughly /tuːn/.
Step 1: The highest long vowel /uː/ changes into a diphthong according to the rule in the figure.
Step 2: Since /uː/ → /aʊ/, it becomes today's /taʊn/.
Interpretation: Words whose spelling ow/ou is read like "ow" (*house*, *cloud*, *town*) form a group that underwent the same change.

examples.title: Interpreting the vowel difference in derived words
body: Given: The vowels differ in *divine* and *divinity*.
Step 1: The long vowel of *divine* went through the Great Vowel Shift and became /aɪ/.
Step 2: In *divinity*, that syllable became short in derivation, leaving /ɪ/, close to the short vowel from before the shift.
Interpretation: The vowel alternation is not arbitrary but the result of historical change, and such relations let us understand a whole family of words at once.

el-12.title: English Phonology: Phonemes, Allophones, and the Three Sounds of -s
explain: The endings of *cats*, *dogs*, and *buses* are all spelled -s, yet we read them with three different sounds. At school you are told to memorize this, but these sounds follow a rule. The rule appears when you look at **sounds**, not spelling. Phonology deals with the system by which sounds are used in a language.

The basic unit is the **phoneme**. It is the smallest unit of sound that distinguishes the meaning of words, and is written between slashes / /. *Pin* and *bin* differ only in the first sounds, /p/ and /b/, and so differ in meaning. A pair of words that differ in only one sound like this is called a **minimal pair**, and if such a pair exists, the two sounds are different phonemes. *Thigh* and *thy* are also a minimal pair for /θ/ and /ð/.

A variant pronunciation of one phoneme depending on the environment is called an **allophone**. The p of *pin* is [pʰ] (aspirated), released with a strong puff of breath, and the p of *spin* is [p], with almost no breath. English speakers hear these two as the same /p/, because swapping the two sounds does not change the meaning. In Korean, the same difference is used to distinguish ㅍ from ㅂ. Which differences are phoneme differences varies from language to language.

Now back to -s. The plural -s is a single morpheme, but it is realized as three **allomorphs**. The rule looks at the preceding sound. (1) If the preceding sound is not **voiced** (/p t k f θ/ and so on), it is /s/: *cats*, *books*. (2) If the preceding sound is voiced (including vowels, /b d g v m n/ and so on), it is /z/: *dogs*, *bees*. (3) If the preceding sound is a sibilant (/s z ʃ ʒ tʃ dʒ/), it is /ɪz/: *buses*, *dishes*, *judges*. (3) is needed because /s/ or /z/ added after the same kind of sound would be hard to hear distinctly.

The past -ed works the same way. After a voiceless sound it is /t/ (*walked*), after a voiced sound it is /d/ (*played*), and after /t, d/ it is /ɪd/ (*wanted*). In both cases the core is the **assimilation** rule of "matching voicing to the neighboring sound." Since there is one rule, English speakers know that adding -s to a word they have never seen, *blick*, would give [s].

Stress also follows phonological rules. English has pairs in which stress distinguishes the part of speech of a word. The noun *RECord* (stress on the first syllable) and the verb *reCORD* (stress on the second syllable), and the noun *PREsent* and the verb *preSENT*, are examples. However, many pairs such as *answer* do not follow this tendency, so it is only a tendency. Sound is not played, so stress is marked with capital letters.

Limits: the rules above are generalizations and have exceptions. Dialects differ in their inventories of phonemes, and the distinction between [ ] and / / above is simplified. Also, not every spelled -s is an allomorph of the plural (the -s of *bus* is part of the root). The habit of dividing into morphemes comes first.

examples.title: Deciding the sound of the plural -s
body: Given: the pronunciation of the plurals of *cap*, *bag*, and *church*.
Step 1: Check the final sound. *Cap* ends in the voiceless /p/, *bag* in the voiced /g/, and *church* in the sibilant /tʃ/.
Step 2: Apply the rule. *Caps* is /s/, *bags* is /z/, and *churches* is /ɪz/.
Interpretation: The spelling is -s in all of them, but the three allomorphs are determined by the preceding sound.

examples.title: Judging whether it is a phoneme or an allophone
body: Given: the [pʰ] of *pin* and the [p] of *spin*.
Step 1: See whether swapping the two sounds changes the meaning. Even if swapped, *pin* is understood as *pin* and *spin* as *spin* (it only sounds slightly odd).

Step 2: Also check complementary environments. The aspirated sound appears at the start of a stressed syllable at the beginning of a word, and the unaspirated sound after /s/, so they are used in different places.
Interpretation: In English, the two sounds are allophones of a single phoneme /p/. /p/ and /b/ change the meaning, as in *pin*/*bin*, so they are separate phonemes.

pairs: when the preceding sound is a voiceless sound like /p, t, k/ (cats)
when the preceding sound is a voiced sound like /g/ (dogs)
when the preceding sound is a sibilant like /s, ʃ, dʒ/ (buses)

checks.explanation: The order is checking the last sound, testing for a sibilant, telling voiced from voiceless, and deciding.

If it is a sibilant, read it as /ɪz/
If it is not a sibilant, tell whether it is voiced or voiceless
If voiced, read /z/; if voiceless, read /s/

options: It is an iron rule that applies without exception to all two-syllable words
There is a tendency for nouns to be stressed on the first syllable and verbs on the second, but there are many exceptions
Nouns and verbs are always spelled differently
Stress has no relation to the meaning of words in English

el-13.title: Shakespearean Drama and Iambic Pentameter
explain: Reading the plays of William Shakespeare (1564-1616), you sense that the characters' lines differ from everyday speech. This is because a large part of these lines is **verse** fitted to a set rhythm. Knowing what kind of rhythm it is and why it was used changes how you read the lines aloud. All the example lines in this lesson are fictional lines written for this course.

The unit of rhythm is the **foot**. The most common foot in English poetry is the **iamb**, a pair in which a weak syllable is followed by a strong one. As in *be-LOW* and *a-WAY*, the two syllables divide into weak-strong. When this foot repeats five times in a line, it is **iambic pentameter**, and the line has ten syllables. Penta means five.

explain.alt: A figure dividing the English line "The morning light came softly through the door" into ten syllables. The syllables are The, mor, ning, light, came, soft, ly, through, the, door, and under each syllable there is alternately a small empty circle (weak syllable) or a large green circle (strong syllable). Five orange brackets, each grouping two syllables, are numbered 1 to 5. Legend: weak syllable, strong syllable, numbers are foot numbers.

explain: The figure shows how to read a line split into ten syllables. Weak syllables (empty circles) and strong ones (green circles) alternate, and the five feet, each grouping two syllables, are numbered. Read aloud, it has the rhythm "da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM..." Everyday English sentences also tend to alternate weak and strong in this way, so iambic pentameter is said to be a rhythm close to the way English is spoken.

**Blank verse** is verse written in iambic pentameter without rhyme at the ends of lines. It is the main verse form of Shakespeare's plays. Rhyming lines are used at the joints of the story. A **couplet**, two lines rhymed together, often comes at the end of a scene and gives a feeling that "the curtain is falling." Ordinary conversation and the lines of comic characters, on the other hand, tend to be written in **prose** rather than verse. The tendency is often explained as verse for noble characters and prose for those of low rank, but there are many scenes in which nobles use prose and commoners use verse, so it is a tendency, not a rule.

Variation is what brings the rhythm to life. Representative examples are **trochaic inversion**, in which a line begins with strong-weak instead of weak-strong, the **feminine ending**, in which an eleventh weak syllable is added, and the **caesura**, a pause in the middle of a line. When the same rhythm repeats and is then broken, the meaning is emphasized, which is a clue for reading.

Let us also learn the conditions of drama as a genre. The theaters of the time had almost no scenery, so the setting was conveyed through the lines. It was the convention to divide a play into five acts, and the soliloquy, in which a character speaks his or her thoughts alone, and the aside, spoken only to the audience, were used. Limits: stress is relative, so the same line can be divided differently depending on the reader, and since pronunciation differed in each period (the Great Vowel Shift in an earlier lesson), a rhythm that fit the old pronunciation may be off when read today.

examples.title: Scanning a line written for this lesson
body: Given: *The river runs beyond the silent hill.*
Step 1: Count the syllables. The(1) riv(2) er(3) runs(4) be(5) yond(6) the(7) si(8) lent(9) hill(10) makes ten syllables.
Step 2: Group them as weak-strong according to the natural stress. The RIV | er RUNS | be YOND | the SI | lent HILL.
Interpretation: Ten syllables with five iambs make iambic pentameter. This unrhymed line could be a line of blank verse.

examples.title: A line with a feminine ending
body: Given: *The summer evening settles on the water.*
Step 1: Count the syllables. The(1) sum(2) mer(3) eve(4) ning(5) set(6) tles(7) on(8) the(9) wa(10) ter(11) makes eleven syllables.
Step 2: Marking the stress gives the SUM | mer EVE | ning SET | tles ON | the WA | ter. One more weak syllable, ter, is attached after the five feet.
Interpretation: The eleventh weak syllable is not an error but a normal variation called the feminine ending. A syllable count other than ten does not mean it is not iambic pentameter.

Five orange brackets, each grouping two syllables, are numbered 1 to 5. Legend: weak syllable, strong syllable, numbers are foot numbers.

el-14.title: Sonnet Form and the Metaphysical Conceit
explain: Can a short fourteen-line poem hold an argument, a reversal, and a conclusion? The **sonnet** is just such a form. It began in Italy, was brought into English in the 16th century by Thomas Wyatt and the Earl of Surrey, and afterward became a representative form of English poetry. A sonnet uses iambic pentameter in fourteen lines and follows a set **rhyme scheme**.

A rhyme scheme is written with letters. Lines with the same letter end in the same sound. The two representative English sonnet forms are shown in the figure below. The **Shakespearean** form is abab cdcd efef gg, that is, three quatrains and a final couplet. The **Petrarchan** form consists of an opening eight lines (the octave) abbaabba and a closing six lines (the sestet) cdecde and so on. The sestet's arrangement has variations, so the figure gives one example.

explain.alt: A figure showing the rhyme symbols of a 14-line poem in two columns. The left, "Shakespearean," has four groups: abab, cdcd, efef, gg (4 lines, 4 lines, 4 lines, 2 lines). The right, "Petrarchan," has eight lines abbaabba (8 lines) and six lines cdecde (6 lines). A note says that the same letter means the same rhyme.

explain: Form is tied to the structure of the argument. A sonnet often has a **volta** (turn). In the Petrarchan form, the problem of the octave turns into the sestet's response at line 9, and in the Shakespearean form, the thought is built up over three quatrains and then turned or summed up in the final couplet (or at line 9). So by reading the rhymes, you can gauge the logical structure of the poem in advance.

Let us practice reading rhymes. Here are four lines written for this course.
- I kept a lamp beside the window sill, (a)
- And watched the dark come slowly down the street; (b)
- The wind went by, the house grew very still, (a)
- And all the night was waiting at my feet. (b)
*Sill* and *still*, and *street* and *feet*, each rhyme, so the scheme is abab. This becomes the first quatrain of a Shakespearean sonnet. Rhyme is judged by **sound, not spelling**. *Love* and *move* are an **eye rhyme**: although their spellings are similar, their sounds do not rhyme.

The poets of the early 17th century such as John Donne (1572-1631), George Herbert, and Andrew Marvell are called the **Metaphysical poets**. This name was spread, with a critical sense, by Samuel Johnson in the 18th century. The characteristic of these poets is the **conceit**: an extended metaphor that links two very different things through unexpected, intellectual logic. Donne is famous for a poem comparing the souls of parting lovers to the two legs of a drawing compass. Its characteristic is working out emotion as if it were an argument. Here is one conceit written for this course: *Our friendship is a bridge built from both banks at once; where the halves meet, we call it trust.*

Limits: when sounds change, old rhymes may not fit when read today. This is because pronunciation changed, as with the Great Vowel Shift in an earlier lesson. Also, English sonnets have variations such as the Spenserian form (ababbcbccdcdee), and modern poets sometimes use the form loosely. Knowing the frame is for reading the points where a poem departs from it.

examples.title: Labeling a rhyme scheme
body: Given: The end words of four lines are, in order, night, more, light, door.
Step 1: Label night in the first line a. More has a different sound, so it is b.
Step 2: Light has the same sound as night, so it is a, and door has the same sound as more, so it is b.
Interpretation: The scheme is abab. It has the same structure as one quatrain of a Shakespearean sonnet.

examples.title: Reading a conceit
body: Given: *Our friendship is a bridge built from both banks at once.*
Step 1: Find the two dissimilar things. They are friendship (abstract) and a bridge (concrete).
Step 2: Read the part where the comparison extends. Being built from both sides at once explains mutuality, and the place where the two halves meet explains trust.
Interpretation: A conceit does not end with a single comparison but continues the details of the bridge like points in an argument.

el-15.title: From Romanticism to Modernist Poetry
explain: In the late 18th century, a few English poets claimed that "poetry comes not from the elegant conversation of the aristocracy but from the feelings and speech of ordinary people." About a hundred years later, other poets said, "Let us not pour out feeling, but set down the image precisely." Comparing these two currents reveals the main line of English poetry. All the example passages in this lesson were written for this course.

**Romanticism** was a current that ran from the late 18th century into the first half of the 19th. In opposition to the reason-centeredness of the Enlightenment and to industrialization, it put feeling, the individual, imagination, and nature first. *Lyrical Ballads*, published by Wordsworth and Coleridge in 1798, is often mentioned as the starting point, and Blake, Byron, Shelley, and Keats followed. The poets differed considerably from one another. Blake liked to use mystical symbolism, and Byron to deal with satire and rebellious characters.

Let us look at four lines in the Romantic manner written for this course.
- O river, carry what I cannot say
- beneath the hills where evening lingers long;
- my thoughts like willow leaves are borne away,
- and nature answers with its silent song.
The speaker's feeling comes to the fore, and nature becomes the addressee. The abab rhyme and the iambic pentameter are regular.

**Modernism** arose in the early 20th century. Faced with the First World War, urbanization, and new technologies, a sense spread that existing forms could not contain reality. Representative attempts include **Imagism** of Ezra Pound, H.D., and others (1910s, emphasizing a single vivid image) and T. S. Eliot's *The Waste Land* (1922, fragmentary composition and allusions to many texts). In America, Walt Whitman, much earlier (1855, *Leaves of Grass*), opened up **free verse**, and Emily Dickinson liked to use **slant rhyme**, in which line-end sounds are similar but do not match completely, along with dashes.

Here are three lines in the Imagist manner written for this course.
- Rain on the tram window —
- a row of small lights
- sliding through the dark.
There is neither rhyme nor regular rhythm. Instead of explaining words, it sets down one concrete image. The line lengths of 6-5-5 syllables come not from an even frame but from the breathing of the image.

**Free verse** is poetry without set meter or rhyme. But "no rules" is different from "no form." Line breaks create the movement of the gaze and pauses, and repetition of sounds creates structure. Even the same sentence changes its emphasis when the lines are changed. Asking where the lines are broken is the starting point of reading free verse.

Limits: the periods overlap. The Victorian era (Tennyson, Browning) and Hopkins stand between the two currents, and Yeats had both a Romantic sensibility and Modernist technique. Some Modernist poets also wrote in fixed forms, and Romantic poets were not always sentimental. A label is the starting point of reading, not a conclusion.

examples.title: Comparing and classifying two poems
body: Given: Compare the four lines introduced earlier (river) and the three lines (rain).
Step 1: Look at the form. River has regular iambic pentameter and abab rhyme, and rain is free verse without rhyme or regular rhythm.
Step 2: Look at the way of speaking. River directly shows the speaker's feeling and communion with nature, and rain presents an image without interpretation.
Interpretation: Each shows the traits of the Romantic manner and the Imagist manner most vividly. However, this one pair cannot represent either movement as a whole.

examples.title: The effect of line breaks
body: Given: Compare writing the same sentence, *Rain on the tram window — a row of small lights sliding through the dark.*, as one line and breaking it into three lines.
Step 1: Written as one line, the image runs on in a single breath and reads like an explanatory sentence.
Step 2: Broken into three lines, *window — / a row of small lights / sliding* produces a short pause and a movement of the gaze, and after *lights* there is a brief stop before the motion continues.
Interpretation: The line breaks determine the order and speed in which the image appears.

el-16.title: The Rise of the English Novel and Narrative Point of View
explain: Old tales and epics dealt with heroes, kings, and miracles. But in 18th-century England there poured out prose stories that followed at length the day and the mind of an ordinary, nameless person. This is the genre we call the novel today. This lesson deals with the background of its appearance and with the first question asked when reading a novel, "Who is telling the story?"

Daniel Defoe's *Robinson Crusoe* (1719), Samuel Richardson's *Pamela* (1740), and Henry Fielding's *Tom Jones* (1749) are commonly counted as early English novels. The literary scholar Ian Watt, in *The Rise of the Novel* (1957), explained the character of this genre as **formal realism**. He meant that it describes realistically an individual with a concrete name, place, and time who goes through everyday events. As background he cited rising literacy, the growth of a middle-class readership, and circulating libraries and periodicals.

Watt's explanation was very influential, but it has also been criticized. Prose tales and romances existed before, and it is pointed out that women writers such as Aphra Behn and Eliza Haywood were overlooked. Also, the question of what the "first novel" is changes with the definition. Some name Spain's *Don Quixote* (1605) or Japan's *The Tale of Genji* (early 11th century) first. Watt's thesis is best learned as one interpretation rather than accepted as the only answer.

Let us first sort out narrative point of view. In **first-person point of view**, an "I" who took part in the story tells it. Knowledge is limited and subjective. In **third-person omniscient point of view**, the narrator knows the inner thoughts of several characters and even the whole of the events. In **third-person limited point of view**, the narration stays within one character's field of view. Even for the same event, what the reader comes to know differs depending on who knows how much. A first-person narrator cannot tell what even he or she does not know, while an omniscient narrator can tell what the character does not know, as in *Jun did not know that the letter had already been sent.*

Jane Austen (1775-1817, best known for *Pride and Prejudice*, 1813) used **free indirect discourse** skillfully. Let us compare three forms. Direct speech: *Mina thought, "I am too tired to go."* Indirect speech: *Mina thought that she was too tired to go.* Free indirect discourse: *Mina looked at the stairs. Too tired, surely, to go up again.* In the last, with neither quotation marks nor *she thought*, the character's thought seeps into the narrator's voice. The reader feels the narrator's and the character's views blend, and reading this boundary is a core skill in reading novels.

In the 19th century, Victorian realist novels flourished, such as Charlotte Brontë's *Jane Eyre* (1847), the novels of Charles Dickens, and George Eliot's (the pen name of Mary Ann Evans) *Middlemarch* (1871-72). In these, an omniscient narrator generally surveys the characters and society broadly and adds moral commentary. Dickens made use of serial publication in magazines, and the serial form affected how events were arranged and tension was controlled.

Limits: the classification of point of view is a convenient frame. Within one work the point of view may shift, or the narrator may not be reliable. Also, narrator and author are not the same. The bias of a first-person narrator is not the author's position. When reading a novel, ask together: "Who is speaking, from where, with how much knowledge, and why in this way?"

examples.title: Telling narrative points of view apart
body: Given: There are three sentences. (a) *I did not see the letter.* (b) *Jun did not know that the letter had already been sent.* (c) *Mina opened the box. Empty again, of course.*
Step 1: (a) is first person, with "I" speaking directly, and (b) has an omniscient narrator, since the narrator tells even a fact Jun does not know.
Step 2: The second sentence of (c) seems to be the narrator's explanation, but Mina's irritation, "again, of course," seeps into it, so it is free indirect discourse.
Interpretation: Depending on the point of view, the range of information the reader knows and the distance from the character change.

examples.title: Converting among direct, indirect, and free indirect discourse
body: Given: Direct speech *Jun thought, "The bus is late again."*
Step 1: Change it to indirect speech. *Jun thought that the bus was late again.* Person and tense shift to the narrator's standpoint.
Step 2: Change it to free indirect discourse. Drop *Jun thought* from *The bus was late again, Jun thought.* and leave the character's manner of speech, as in *The bus was late again. Typical.*
Interpretation: As the quotation marks disappear, the narrator's and the character's voices blend.

el-17.title: The Modernist Novel and Narrative Time
explain: Victorian novels followed several decades in the life of a family. But in the early 20th century there appeared novels that treat a single day, sometimes just a few hours, over hundreds of pages. James Joyce's *Ulysses* (1922) deals with one day in Dublin, June 16, 1904, and Virginia Woolf's *Mrs Dalloway* (1925) with one day in London. If a story can be short while the text grows long, we have to divide "time" into two layers.

Narratology divides a narrative into two layers. **Story** is the events as they happened in actual chronological order, and **discourse** is the way they are arranged and conveyed in the text. Gérard Genette examined the relation between the two in terms of **order**, **duration**, and **frequency**. Order concerns whether the arrangement of events is chronological (flashback, foreshadowing), duration concerns the ratio between story time and the amount of text, and frequency concerns how many times an event that happened once is told.

explain.alt: A two-bar figure. The upper bar is story time, with segments A 1 hour, B 3 hours, C 1 hour, D 5 hours, and E 2 hours in sequence. The lower bar is the amount of text, with the same segments A 40 pages, B 30 pages, C 80 pages, D 30 pages, and E 20 pages in sequence. Segments with the same letter are joined by dotted lines, and a note says it is a fictional novel covering a day from 8 o'clock to 20 o'clock.

explain: The figure shows a fictional novel covering a day from 8 o'clock to 20 o'clock. The upper bar is story time, and the lower bar is the amount of text. Let us read duration through ratios. Segment A packs 1 hour into 40 pages (40 pages per hour), and segment C narrates most slowly, at 80 pages for 1 hour. Segment D compresses 5 hours into 30 pages, which is 6 pages per hour. The more pages per hour, the more it feels as though story time is flowing slowly.

Genette divides duration into four kinds. A **scene** is narration in which story time and the length of text are about equal (such as dialogue), a **summary** is narration that compresses a long time into a short one, a **pause** is narration in which story time stops while description or commentary continues, and an **ellipsis** is a case where the passage of time is skipped in the text. In the figure, segment D corresponds to summary, and segment C to slow narration in which events are concentrated into one hour.

The Modernist novel used these devices radically. **Stream of consciousness** is a technique in which a character's thoughts follow one another as they arise, without grammatical tidying. An example written for this course: *Bus late. Again. The clock on the corner says ten past — no, it is always fast. Tea, then, or the letter? The letter.* Sentences break off and thoughts change direction. Joseph Conrad's *Heart of Darkness* uses a **frame narrative**, in which a narrator named Marlow conveys the story. **Multiple points of view**, which show one event through the eyes of several characters, and the **unreliable narrator**, whom the reader must doubt (a concept Wayne Booth set out in 1961), are also closely related to this period.

Limits: the ratio of pages to time is only a tool for estimating the feel of reading and does not measure the actual reading experience as it is. The same number of pages can have different numbers of characters and sentence lengths. Also, the name "Modernist novel" is a classification centered on the English-speaking world and does not always coincide with experiments in other regions at the same time. Nor is every Modernist novel difficult.

examples.title: Comparing duration by pages per hour
body: Given: In the figure, segment B is 30 pages for 3 hours, and segment E is 20 pages for 2 hours.
Step 1: The pages per hour for B are 30 ÷ 3 = 10.
Step 2: For E it is 20 ÷ 2 = 10. The speeds of the two segments are the same.
Interpretation: The total lengths differ but the narration speed is the same. To compare speed, look at the ratio, not the amount.

Step 1: Compare the order of the text with the order of events. The first scene is the last in terms of events.
Step 2: The reader sees the result first and learns the cause later.
Interpretation: Manipulating order creates tension and irony. For example, once you know the ending, a trivial action in an earlier scene looks different.

el-18.title: Postcolonialism and Contemporary Critical Theory
explain: Even after reading the same novel, different people say different things. One takes up the structure of the sentences, another the class of the characters, and yet another who is unable to speak. **Critical theory** is a frame that asks such questions systematically. It is not a formula that gives the right answer, but a lens that determines what you are made to see in a text.

explain.alt: A list of five lenses and representative questions. Formalism: how do form and image create meaning? Reader-response: how does the reader make meaning while reading? Marxism: how are class and economic relations revealed? Feminism: how do gender power and representation work? Postcolonialism: who speaks of the legacy of colonial rule, and how?

explain: Let us unpack the five lenses in the figure. The **New Criticism** (formalism) of the mid-20th century valued the form within the text over the author's life. Wimsatt and Beardsley's "The Intentional Fallacy" (1946) is the representative discussion. **Reader-response criticism** holds that meaning is made in the reader's process of reading. **Marxist criticism** looks at how class and economic relations are reflected in literature. **Feminist criticism** asks about gender power and the representation of women (Gilbert and Gubar's *The Madwoman in the Attic*, 1979). And then there is **postcolonial criticism**.

**Postcolonialism** asks about the traces that the history of colonial rule and its legacy have left in literature, culture, and knowledge. In *Orientalism* (1978), Edward Said analyzed the discourse in which the West has constructed "the Orient" as a stagnant, exotic Other. Gayatri Spivak raised the problem of lower groups (the subaltern) who are not given the chance to speak, and Homi Bhabha discussed the hybridity that arises when two cultures meet. As in the title of *The Empire Writes Back* (1989), there is also the view that writers from the colonies use English but write back in a new voice.

Chinua Achebe's *Things Fall Apart* (1958) is a representative case. It portrays Igbo society in Nigeria from within, and narrates in English, together with Igbo proverbs, the changes before and after the arrival of Europeans. Achebe also criticized, in a 1975 lecture, the way European novels had portrayed Africa. In this way, a postcolonial reading asks, "Through whose eyes is this story told?"

Let us practice with a fictional text written for this course. It is a passage from the diary of a traveler visiting a colony. *The islanders have no writing, so they cannot tell their own history; I record it for them.* The order of reading is this. (1) Identify the claim: the narrator presupposes that the islanders cannot speak for themselves. (2) Identify the grounds: is the link from "have no writing" to "cannot tell their history" valid? (3) Apply the lens: who holds the authority of the record, and where is the islanders' voice? Doubting the narrator's assumptions in this way is a postcolonial reading.

Interpretation needs discipline. Whatever lens is used, the structure of **claim-evidence-inference** must be kept. That is, you must cite a specific passage from the text as evidence and explain why it supports the claim. To say that several interpretations are possible does not mean that any interpretation is right. As a limit, the lenses overlap (gender, class, and colonial rule work together), and applying theory mechanically risks reducing the text to an example of the theory.

examples.title: Choosing a lens by its questions
body: Given (hypothetical): In a certain novel, the maid has almost no lines, and there is no mention of the pay for the work she does.
Step 1: Put what stands out into words. "Who speaks and who stays silent, and how is the pay for labor hidden?"
Step 2: Compare it with the questions in the figure. "How are class and economic relations revealed?" is the closest.
Interpretation: The Marxist lens comes to mind first. Since the maid is a woman, the feminist lens can be used as well, so lenses may overlap.

examples.title: Writing claim-evidence-inference
body: Given: Read the passage *I record it for them.* from the traveler's diary.
Step 1: Write the claim. "The narrator sets himself up as the spokesman of the islanders and erases their voice."

Step 2: Write the evidence and the inference. The evidence is the contrast between *cannot tell their own history* and *I record it for them*. The inference is that this sentence presupposes as fact that they "cannot speak," and on that premise grants the authority to record to himself.
Interpretation: When a claim, evidence, and inference are all present even for a single sentence, an impression becomes an argument.

el-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Reading One Text in Many Layers
explain: So far we have learned separately the sentence structure of English, the history and phonology of English, poetry and drama, and the novel and criticism. In an actual text, all these layers work at the same time. The task of this lesson is training in putting a short text in front of you and asking, "What can be seen at which layer?"

Let us set out the order of analysis. (1) **Sentence layer**: sentence structure, tense, non-finite phrases, information structure, the passive, and so on. Who is the subject, and what is placed at the end of the sentence? (2) **Word and sound layer**: the lineage of words (everyday or academic), repetition of sounds, whether the rhymes hold. (3) **Form layer**: the rhythm of the lines, the rhyme scheme, forms such as the sonnet, or the narrative speed of prose. (4) **Narration layer**: who speaks and how much he or she knows. (5) **Interpretation layer**: through what lens will you read, and what evidence will you cite?

The practice text is the four lines we saw earlier.
- I kept a lamp beside the window sill,
- And watched the dark come slowly down the street;
- The wind went by, the house grew very still,
- And all the night was waiting at my feet.
At the sentence layer, finite clauses in the past tense continue consistently, and the lines are joined by coordination (*And*). At the word layer, there are many short basic words from Old English onward, such as *wind, house, night, feet*, which create an everyday tone. At the form layer, it is ten-syllable iambic pentameter with abab rhyme. At the narration layer, a first-person speaker tells only what he or she saw from his or her own room.

Connecting the layers deepens the interpretation. Simple sentences of short words and coordination, and the regular rhythm, create the stillness of night settling slowly. The *waiting* and *feet* of the last line create a personification in which the night waits for the person. Going step by step in this way, "structure → effect → interpretation," is close reading.

When reading old texts, one must take sound change into account. A rhyme that does not hold today may have held in the old pronunciation, and conversely a rhyme that holds today may have failed in the old pronunciation. Such judgments need knowledge of the history of English and phonology. Not losing the understood subject in a long sentence built with non-finite clauses, and deciding whether the narrator is omniscient or limited in point of view, are likewise part of the same synthesis.

Limits: analysis by layers is a tool for cutting the text apart, so in the end you must put it back together and read it whole. Also, rich analysis does not settle the interpretation into one. The standard of persuasiveness is to state the evidence and the inference you used.

examples.title: Layer-by-layer analysis of the four-line poem
body: Given: the four lines of the lamp poem above.
Step 1: Form layer. Counting syllables gives ten in each line, and the iamb repeats five times, so it is iambic pentameter. The rhymes are sill-still and street-feet, abab.
Step 2: Narration layer. A first-person speaker tells only the scene seen from inside the room and does not report circumstances in the outside world.
Interpretation: The regular rhythm suits the calm progress of the night, and the limited first-person point of view strengthens the lonely atmosphere.

examples.title: Finding an error at the sentence layer
body: Given: *Opening the door, the room felt cold.*
Step 1: Find the understood subject of *Opening*. The subject of the main clause is the room.
Step 2: It would mean the room opens the door, so it is a dangling participle. Fix it as in *Opening the door, I felt the room was cold.*
Interpretation: In an integrated problem, it is safe to check structural problems at the sentence layer first, before form and theme.
