el-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Close Reading of an English Literary Text
explain:
The capstone is a task in which you apply the tools of English linguistics and literature learned so far directly to one text. The subject is the short prose passage below. It is a fictional text written for this course, and a plain paraphrase is given with it.
*Nobody in the village could say when the clock on the church tower had stopped. It showed ten past four, and that was enough for the old women, who told the time by the shadows instead. "It is always ten past four somewhere," the baker used to say, handing over the warm bread. But the new schoolteacher, who had come from the city with a watch on each wrist, found the stopped clock hard to forgive. She looked up at it every morning, and every morning it looked back, patient and wrong.*
Paraphrase: No one in the village could say when the church tower clock had stopped. It pointed to ten past four, and that was good enough for the old women, who read the time from shadows. The baker used to say, handing over warm bread, that ten past four is always the right time somewhere. But the new teacher from the city, wearing a watch on each wrist, could hardly forgive the stopped clock. Every morning she looked up at it, and every morning it looked back at her, patient and wrong.

First read the **sentence layer**. The first sentence holds a long noun clause, in *Nobody ... could say when ...*. In the second sentence, *who told the time by the shadows instead* is a relative clause that adds, as new information, that the old women use shadows instead of the clock. The opening of the second sentence, *It showed ten past four*, sets the clock up as the subject. This sentence structure fits the sense that the village's gaze pushes the clock aside as a standard. The last sentence creates **symmetry** with *She looked up ..., and every morning it looked back*, and puts the closing *patient and wrong* in end-focus position.

**Word and sound layer**: everyday, concrete words such as *shadows*, *bread*, and *tower* create the texture of the village. *Forgive*, on the other hand, is a moral word, which makes the stopped clock be treated like a being that has committed a wrong. The repetition of *ten past four* fixes the stopped time in sound as well.

**Narration layer**: the narrator is third person and is close to omniscient in that he or she knows both the general circumstances of the village (the old women, the baker) and the teacher's inner mind (*found the stopped clock hard to forgive*). In the last sentence, *patient and wrong* produces the effect of **free indirect discourse**, in which the boundary blurs between whether it is the narrator's comment or the teacher's thought. **Theme layer**: two ways of measuring time are contrasted, the shadow (natural time) and two wristwatches (mechanical time). A dichotomy of village against city, slowness against precision can be read.

Now the **interpretation layer**. Let us choose one lens. For example, read through a postcolonial or Marxist lens, the teacher from the city becomes a gaze that takes "precise time" as the norm and tries to correct the village. Read through a formalist lens, one points out the duality the contradictory pair of adjectives *patient and wrong* gives to the clock. Whatever lens is used, **claim-evidence-inference** must be present.

The evaluation criteria are as follows. (1) Are the observations of sentence, word, and narration concrete? (2) Do the observations lead to interpretation? (3) Does the argument keep to one lens consistently? (4) Does it acknowledge limits? As a limit, this text is one short paragraph, so the author's intention and wider context cannot be known, and the interpretation is valid only within the evidence of this passage. Of the two questions in this task, the writing question is a self-check against a model answer, and the submission question is not scored.

examples.title: Close reading of one sentence
body: Given: *She looked up at it every morning, and every morning it looked back, patient and wrong.*
Step 1: Observe the structure. Two clauses are joined by and, and *every morning* is repeated twice. The subject She of the first clause and the subject it of the second clause trade places.

Step 2: Infer the effect. The repetition and the swap of subjects create a face-to-face between the teacher and the clock. The closing patient and wrong becomes the focus and leaves an evaluation of the clock ("patient but wrong").
Interpretation: The clock is raised from an object to a counterpart that looks back, and the position of the teacher, who takes precision as the highest value, is shaken.

examples.title: Building a claim-evidence-inference paragraph
body: Given: The claim "This text contrasts precise time with the village's notion of time."
Step 1: Choose two pieces of evidence. The old women *told the time by the shadows*, and the teacher has *a watch on each wrist*.

Step 2: Write the inference. The shadow symbolizes natural time that follows the sun and the wristwatch mechanical time, and the contrast between a village for which one clock is enough and a teacher wearing two watches condenses the difference between the two notions.
Interpretation: If after quoting the evidence you always write "so what is being contrasted," the paragraph becomes an argument.

checks.hint: Look at the repeated expression, the swap of subjects, and the end of the sentence.

checks.model: The sentence repeats every morning twice and swaps the subject She of the first clause with the subject it of the second, creating a symmetrical structure in which the teacher and the clock face each other.
